title: The US Navy Ran Itself Into the Ground, and the Next Crisis May Have No Carrier to Send
dek: Three years of high-intensity Middle East deployments have burned through ships and people: for the next few years there may be only one carrier at sea at any given time, and adversaries are watching that gap.
why: The first half on the mechanics and numbers of naval readiness is solid; the second half on AI cyberwar and PLA Rocket Force anti-corruption is open-ended discussion. Information density is moderate.
who: Investors and researchers tracking US military readiness, Taiwan Strait and European defense scenarios, plus engineers making judgments on AI safety and cyber offense-defense.
skip: The last ten minutes or so of Rocket Force anti-corruption doggerel and book chat can be skipped.

points.h: The US Navy ran itself into the ground
points.body: Brian's judgment: over the past three years, from the Houthis to Iran to Israel and Iran, the US concentrated a fleet normally dispersed around the globe into the Middle East, and nearly every ship that went to sea had its deployment extended. The result is equipment breaking and people breaking, and a great reset is now unavoidable — at any point in the next few years there may be only one carrier at sea, and the number of destroyers available may be only half of normal deployment levels. So despite the current shipbuilding boom, in the near term the Navy is ‘on one knee.’ This is not defeat; it is exhaustion from its own operational tempo.

points.h: What broke is not morale, it is generators and steam lines
points.body: One layer down, what specifically breaks is mechanical systems: the engine rooms of nuclear-powered carriers still run on steam, with many moving parts that wear out; one destroyer was stranded in the South China Sea for several days after a generator failure knocked out power. Maintenance falls behind because the ships are at sea, and the less they are maintained the more easily they break. The human side is equally concrete: carrier flight operations normally run one shift a day (day or night), and it takes two carriers rotating to sustain continuous operations, which means flight deck crews work 12 hours a day for more than 200 days straight. The supply chain is broken too — there is no port to dock at in the Middle East, so cargo must first be shipped to Diego Garcia and then transferred to the ship, and what sailors end up eating is emergency rations.

points.h: ‘They signed up for it’ does not hold up
points.body: Against the argument that soldiers are supposed to endure hardship, the show offers a rebuttal from personal experience: a first deployment originally set for six months was extended to nine, then twelve, and finally fifteen. The real damage is not the hardship but being repeatedly told ‘you're going home soon’ and then repeatedly delayed. Harder still: some jobs aboard ship have no backup, no third person trained in the same air traffic control role, so even if an immediate family member dies, the person cannot leave. This points directly at reenlistment rates — most of these carrier sailors are on five-year contracts, and after this deployment exactly half of them face the decision of whether to re-up.

points.h: They recruited the people but they cannot get them through the training pipeline
points.body: The Navy struggled to recruit in recent years and only met its goal last year by lowering standards, but those it brought in cannot pass the training school curriculum, so the gaps in the fleet remain — there are currently about 20,000 unfilled sea-duty billets. Retention is holding for now, but a large number of people are said to plan to ‘vote with their feet’ after this deployment. The show connects this to autonomy: the recruiting crisis, not how cool the technology is, is the real driver pushing the military toward unmanned forces.

points.h: Going back to steam catapults is a step backward
points.body: The president wants to cut the electromagnetic systems on new carriers and return to steam catapults and hydraulic elevators. Shashank concedes this is not purely aesthetic: a decade ago EMALS really was badly troubled, delayed and unreliable, and GAO reports document it. But a decade later the situation has changed — the Ford has accumulated roughly 35,000 electromagnetic catapult shots, with more than 12,000 in its most recent record-setting deployment, and the system is working normally. Switching back to steam would mean redesigning the hull to route steam lines, reconfiguring the internal structure, and losing the manpower the Ford saved by converting galley and other steam equipment to electric — equivalent to putting 500 people back on the ship and spending another $10 billion. The next carrier, Doris Miller, could be delayed by four years as a result, delivering close to 2040.

points.h: The maintenance backlog will eat surge capacity in a crisis
points.body: Every ship whose deployment was extended will need a longer-than-normal maintenance period once back in port, eight months to a year; and there is only one shipyard on each coast that can do carrier maintenance, so the queue will pile up. The result is a repeat of the situation three or four years ago: only one carrier deployed for most of the year. What really matters is the crisis scenario — if something happens in the Taiwan Strait, these carriers may not have entered maintenance yet and can only sail with faults: catapults down, arresting gear not working, elevator problems, fewer sorties and fewer aircraft embarked, escorts not at full mission capability, more vulnerable to being hit, and being hit digs the maintenance hole even deeper.

points.h: Munitions, shipbuilding and maintenance add up to one fragile window
points.body: Shashank pulls several threads together: not just redesigns and stalled production lines, but a catastrophic state of munitions stockpiles and the maintenance backlog, and in aggregate the US is entering a ‘perceived window of vulnerability.’ Five, six, seven years ago people were already discussing what the end of this decade would look like and which factors stacking up would make adversaries conclude the US had entered a weak period, and now those factors have been significantly amplified. He links this to John Ratcliffe's trip to Moscow: one possible reading is that Russian intelligence believes the US is unable to respond adequately to a European crisis — at least on missile defense, he does not think the Russians are entirely wrong.

points.h: Cyberwar may escalate from tactical to strategic
points.body: The show cites Michael Sulmeyer's argument: cyber operations have so far failed to deliver the ‘cyber Pearl Harbor’ that was expected. Former UK NCSC head Kieran Martin's formulation is that everyone thought Stuxnet was the future, but maybe it was more like the moon landing — a one-off, resource-intensive feat rather than a routine weekly operation. Cyber is very useful in joint operations (blacking out Caracas, helping disrupt Syrian air defenses), but on its own it is not enough to decide a war at acceptable cost. Sulmeyer argues agentic AI removes the main constraint — the ceiling on what cyber operators can do. In the Hugging Face attack, the 1,200 agents were not themselves there for malicious activity; the malice was a byproduct, yet it was enough to swamp defenses.

points.h: Nobody dares call the offense-defense balance this time
points.body: Shashank says explicitly that he has no answer: in military affairs people argue endlessly over whether technology favors offense or defense. Drones initially looked offense-favoring (Nagorno-Karabakh), but 2022 to 2025 clearly showed that under current conditions defense has the advantage, making offensive maneuver harder. The cyber domain may be the opposite — if the most frontier models are opened only to a few privileged actors, defenders can also use agentic swarms to defend, patch and repair systems without being swamped, in which case defense has the advantage. His conclusion: you have to see how these capabilities are fielded before you can judge, and the drone experience should make us wary of any confident prediction.
